And... puzzle find today - a Sunday from May 16, 2010 by Matt Ginsberg with the title: "Double Crossers." The puzzle had 10 rebus squares that were... quite unusual. Each of those squares had 4 letters embedded that caused the crossing answer to be repeated with the alternate letters. Some examples: FA(ST)ER FA(TH)ER INTHE(RE)D INTHE(EN)D CH(EA)TER CH(AT)TER CONT(RI)TION CONT(EN)TION And those squares worked in the 'down' order for the down answers. A couple of examples: (RE)STITUTION (IN)STITUTION PICK(LE) PICK(ER) Pretty amazing. Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=5/16/2010 ...

If I may wax pedantic--or perhaps, indulge in a little waxy pedantry--for a moment: Now, we all know that the "correct"* plural of "moose"** is "moose"**, and, were I writing a scholarly article on the Cervidae, that is exactly the form I would use. But linguistics is not about correctness, it's about usage--the difference between "prescriptive" and "descriptive"--and a comprehensive dictionary should reflect that. So, I was shooketh--shooketh!--to discover that neither M-W nor the OED mention the form "meese", even labeled "var. joc", even though it's certainly been used ion print/broadcast/on-line media--look! I did it just there! (The OED has a few alternative listings for "meese," including archaic/regional variants of "mice" ((the animals)) and "moss" ((the plant)) ). They may not have meese in Letterkenny, ON, but they certainly have gooses: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w1exJGPZyhs and I suggest you let that one marinate! *Those quotes are pretty scary, aren't they? **Those quotes aren't nearly as scary (although if I were standing in front of a herd of stampeding mxxse, I'd be a little on edge).

So the plate is home plate, between the right- and left-hand batter's boxes. Someone "at the plate" is up to bat. A BUNT is when you just position your bat squarely across the plate and just tap the ball, hopefully not too close to any fielder. The purpose of the BUNT could be an attempt at a hit, if the fielders are playing back (farther from the plate than usual) or leaning toward the other side of the field, or if the batter is especially adept at BUNTing and is very fast. But usually, with runners on base, a BUNT is a sacrifice play, moving one or more runners up one base and closer to scoring. This is because on a good bunt, the safest play is always to first base. Here's some top-tier sacrifice BUNTing: https://www.facebook.com/reel/26886525530983492 And here are some BUNTs for a base hit: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/Cv5v6joPPOw

@Andrzej The family Cervidae, commonly referred to as "the deer family", consists of 23 genera containing 47 species (quoting from animal diversity.org ). And yes, moose are in that biological family.
